title: Data Cache is moving to Runtime Cache
excerpt: Data Cache is exiting beta and moving to Runtime Cache . Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache will switch over on every version without code changes. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own Runtime Cache storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage. Once your team migrates, Data Cache reads and writes that were previously unbilled are charged at Runtime Cache pricing . Rates start at $0.40 per million read units and $4.00 per million write units, and vary by region. Hobby teams get 1 million read units and 200,000 write units free each month across all projects. On Pro, usage draws from your $20 infrastructure credit each month, and anything beyond it is billed at regional rates. For Enterprise pricing, contact your account team. Migration Teams created on or after October 30, 2026 use Runtime Cache by default. If your team already uses Data Cache: Hobby: We’ll migrate your team on November 29, 2026. Pro: We’ll notify you of your migration date and when billing changes take effect. Enterprise: Your account team will contact you with migration details. Before you migrate, review your project's Data Cache usage in Observability . To cut unnecessary reads and writes, follow the optimization guide or copy the agent prompt into your coding agent. In the Runtime Cache dashboard, you can also select Optimize with Vercel Agent. Starting October 30, existing Hobby and Pro teams can opt in early from your team's CDN settings . Runtime Cache pricing applies as soon as you opt in. You can also disable fetch and unstable_cache caching in CDN settings, which sends more requests to your data sources but doesn’t stop your migration. Read about the architecture and recent improvements in the blog post . Read more
summary: Vercel's Data Cache is becoming Runtime Cache, and Hobby teams move over automatically on November 29, 2026. Once moved, cache use that was free before will be billed at per-use rates, with Hobby getting a free monthly allowance.

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
excerpt: Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache , you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations. Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate. Why we built Runtime Cache Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache . Unlike CDN caching , which stores complete HTTP responses, it caches the data used to produce them. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor. We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions . Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps. Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote' , which caches function and component outputs. How Runtime Cache works The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data. Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys. On a miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy. Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale. For example, an application can tag cached product data with catalog . When the catalog changes, invalidating catalog records one timestamp, whether the tag covers one entry or a million. The service doesn’t need to find and delete every matching entry. The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN , distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds. Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions. What we’ve shipped Faster reads during traffic bursts Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available. We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh. We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped. More storage and fewer evictions When a cache exceeds its storage budget, Runtime Cache evicts its least recently used entries, even if they haven’t reached their expiration tim
summary: Vercel is merging its Data Cache into Runtime Cache, so one product now handles data caching. Existing Next.js caching code keeps working without changes, and Pro and Enterprise projects get more storage.

title: Introducing Geist Serif
excerpt: Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens. Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif . Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices. Same system, new voice At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu. A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar . From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print. Display first Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit , which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley. When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go. Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices. From the first prototype to today The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today. Geist grew teeth The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures. The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.” Four families, one x-height Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size. Metric Geist Sans Geist Serif UPM 1000 1000 Cap height 710 710 x-height 530 530 Ascender 710 750 Descender -150 -200 Four variants, one axis Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape ( ELSH ), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart. Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings : Crafted by hand In July the font had 227 glyphs . It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g , for example, is tilted exactly 7°. Specs at a glance Geist Serif ships with: 1 weight (Regular) 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart) 894 glyphs 5 stylistic sets ( ss0
summary: Vercel has released Geist Serif, a new headline typeface that joins its Geist family of fonts. It is built to look sharp on modern screens and suits magazine-style and editorial designs.

title: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
excerpt: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection . Your origin stays private, while web application firewall ( WAF ), caching , bot management , and Workers work just as they do for public origins. In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin. Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers. What is generally available today During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group. Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins: WAF and managed rules Bot management Rate limiting Caching Transform and rewrite rules Workers Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Dedicated CDN Egress IPs aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing . See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations. Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN , no connector software on the origin is required. With Cloudflare Mesh , a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins. How it works Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually. The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network. The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error. What the API looks like For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record. POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true } Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path: { "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true } The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec , GRE , Cloudflare Tunnel , CNI , or Cloudflare Mesh. The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail. Get started Before you begin, you’ll need: The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on. Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh . Unified Routing enabled on your account, unless you connect over Cloudflare Tunnel (Tunnel doesn't need it). Ne
summary: Cloudflare now lets websites and apps that sit on private networks use its protection tools, like firewall, bot blocking, and caching, without opening them to the public internet. Traffic reaches the private service over the company's existing private connection.

title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
excerpt: On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems. Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar , TÜRKTRUST , and TrustWave ), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept. eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key. How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure. Patching Cloudflare Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on. We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora , responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week. Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network? To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21. At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched. About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizat
summary: Cloudflare found that eMudhra, a certificate authority, used extremely weak signing keys, letting anyone rebuild them from public certificates. Cloudflare patched its systems within days and logged about 22,000 attempts to use the weak keys, mostly tests.

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
excerpt: On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response. Faster cold starts Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts: The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag. Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request. In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster. After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms. Usage reporting no longer extends function duration The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration. Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application: Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation . Read more
summary: Vercel's flags tool now starts up about 7 times faster when a server wakes up, cutting wait time from over 70 ms to 10 ms in internal tests. It also no longer makes functions run longer after sending a reply, which can lower usage costs.

title: Vercel Connect adds webhook triggers for more providers
excerpt: Vercel Connect now supports webhook triggers for Resend , X , Twilio , Notion , and Telegram . Connect receives webhook events, such as Telegram bot messages or emails received by your Resend domain, and forwards them to an endpoint in your Vercel project. It verifies incoming requests and handles provider heartbeats and verification challenges for you. To get started: Open Vercel Connect in the dashboard. Enable triggers when creating a connector for your provider or in an existing connector’s settings. Connect registers webhooks automatically for Resend and Telegram. For Twilio, Notion, and X, use the webhook URL from Connect and follow its instructions to complete setup in the provider’s settings. Add a trigger destination to choose the project and endpoint that should receive events. You can turn triggers on or off later in the connector’s settings. In the connector’s Observability tab, select Live to watch incoming trigger events. These connectors join existing trigger support for Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, and Linear. Learn more in the Connect triggers documentation . Read more

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
excerpt: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions . This release includes: HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch ( Undici 8 ) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP. Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support. V8 version 14.6 , the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing. Using Node.js 26 Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects. Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20 , your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment. Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy. Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions. HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy. Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions. Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more. Read more
summary: Node.js 26, a long-term-support version of the tool that runs JavaScript on servers, is now available on Vercel and is the default for new projects. It can reduce wait times when apps call other services, and existing projects upgrade automatically if their settings allow it.

To use Mistral Large 4 in fx, Pi, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or other harnesses, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Then select mistral/mistral-large-4 in the agent. title: IP geolocation now covers more visitors at higher resolution
excerpt: IP geolocation on Vercel now resolves visitor locations with finer network granularity, delivering city-level data for nearly all requests and postal-code data for 90% of traffic. Geolocation data is now refreshed more often, so locations keep up as IP ranges are reassigned and routing changes. This is enabled for all projects with no code or configuration changes required. Existing geolocation headers along with the geolocation() helper in @vercel/functions , return the same fields for Vercel Functions and Routing Middleware . If you use geolocation for access controls, localization, or compliance, some visitors will now resolve to a different city or country, most often traffic from VPNs, hosting providers, and leased IP ranges: Physical termination location: Subnets announced from a hosting provider in a different country than their regional internet registry (RIR) record now resolve to the data center where the traffic actually terminates. Testing geo-dependent routes: Verify access rules against an IP's active network location rather than its static registry allocation. Read the request headers documentation for all available geolocation headers and fields. Read more
summary: Vercel now shows visitor locations with more detail, mostly city-level and postal-code data, and refreshes them more often. It turns on automatically, but some VPN and hosting-provider visitors may now appear in a different country or city than before.

title: Control AI crawlers and assistants separately in Vercel Firewall
excerpt: You can now log or block requests from AI crawlers and AI assistants separately with the AI Bots managed ruleset in Vercel Firewall . AI crawlers: bots that collect content for indexing and model training AI assistants: bots that fetch pages in response to user actions or search queries For example, you can block AI crawlers while allowing AI assistants to retrieve your content to answer users’ questions. Vercel updates the rules as new bots are added. To configure these controls, open your project’s Security > Firewall > Rules . Under Bot Management , enable AI Bots and select the gear icon beside it. Set an action for AI crawlers and AI assistants, then review and publish your changes. You can also modify these rule settings using the Vercel CLI: type: embedded-entry-inline id: 30azXU4HVTfrsO9MbBOCLv Review the changes with vercel firewall diff , then apply them with vercel firewall publish . The AI Bots managed ruleset is available on all plans. Learn more in the documentation . Read more
summary: Vercel's firewall now lets site owners log or block AI crawlers (bots that collect content for training) separately from AI assistants (bots that fetch pages to answer a user's question). This means you can, for example, block training bots while still letting assistants read your pages.

title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
excerpt: Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests). Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production. Our paper, “ Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests. Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale. Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests . More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) , a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch. In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives. The Advantage of Catching JiTTests Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not. Table 1. Key differences between traditional LLM-based code review and Catching JiTTests. How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives). It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers? To address this, we developed two tandem workflows: An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points. A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”). Figure 1. The architecture of the dodgy diff and intent-aware workflows for Catching JiTTests. To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives. We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch. How It Works The entire system workflow happens in five stages: Stage 1: Targeting and Triggering The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism sim
summary: Meta has moved its Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) out of research and into production. The system uses AI to write tests for each proposed code change, aiming to catch bugs before they reach users, with fewer false alarms.

title: Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
excerpt: Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One , Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network . Key insights Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure. Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods. Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggling geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, and contentious domestic events. At the same time, the operational focus shifted away from media organizations toward a wider array of industry targets, including consumer services, Internet infrastructure, and adult entertainment. Q3 by the numbers: 8,200 DDoS attacks every hour Across its network in the third quarter of 2026, Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests. That works out to approximately 8,226 network-layer DDoS attacks per hour, or about 197,400 per day — one attack every 0.44 seconds. The quarter's mitigated traffic totaled 272.6 PB at the network layer and 95.1 PB at the HTTP layer. More swarms, fewer giants Short-burst, mid-range, high-count attacks — the operational signature of DDoS-for-hire "booter" services — accelerated this quarter. These attacks primarily targeted computer software, gambling and casinos, and information technology industries. Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks in Q3 2026, a +208% increase from the same quarter in 2025 : 96% ended in under 10 minutes 98% stayed under 1 Gbps, more than enough to overwhelm a server or website On the other hand, network-level hyper-volumetric attacks (those exceeding 1 Tbps) reversed course, dropping to 251 attacks in Q3 from 805 in Q2 — coinciding with law enforcement action in early 2026 that dismantled four of the largest IoT DDoS botnets: Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad. Still, IoT-based botnets remain a durable high-volume threat as the ecosystem churns through new variants such as Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot . Mirai -classified mitigation peaked in August at 57.23 PB, representing 46.5% of all mitigated network-layer bytes in Q3, including four days — August 16, 19, 23, and 25 — that each cleared three petabytes. The quarter's longest sustained Mirai attack ran 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21. Vector shifts: the collapse of CLDAP and rise of UDP The most dramatic vector shift of the quarter was downward. CLDAP (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) attacks — where small queries with a forged victim IP address trick public domain controllers (UDP 389) into reflecting massive, amplified responses back at the target — experienced a dramatic +580% quarter-over-quarter surge in the first half of the year before collapsing to just 0.05% of attacks in Q3. summary: Cloudflare's Q3 2026 report says tiny, short attacks under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps jumped 208%, while huge attacks over 1 Tbps fell about 69% after police shut down four major botnets. Attackers also switched methods, dropping one attack type almost entirely and using DNS and UDP floods more.

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
excerpt: Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway . A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent . You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents. Use virtual models to: Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them. Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention . Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model. To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model . Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save. Or create one with the Vercel CLI : To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/<slug> , such as vmc/coding-agent . For coding agents , connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration. Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation . Read more
summary: Vercel's AI Gateway now lets you save a model setup under a custom name, like vmc/coding-agent. Apps and agents use that name, so you can change the model or settings in one place without redeploying or reconfiguring them.

title: Vercel Agent can now validate alerts before paging
excerpt: Vercel Agent can now investigate alerts from Vercel monitors before they reach your paging system. With validation enabled for a webhook destination, only alerts Agent classifies as Critical are sent to it. To enable validation: Open a monitor’s notification settings and create or link a webhook destination for your paging system, such as incident.io. Select Critical Only next to that destination. You can also configure notification destinations with the Vercel CLI using vercel monitors notifications . Add --critical-only when linking or updating a webhook destination. Agent checks logs and metrics to assess impact. For example, it can identify health-check errors that don’t affect customers or confirm sustained 5xx errors affecting checkout requests. You can also add context to each monitor to guide Agent’s investigation. Alert validation is available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus. Observability Plus includes ten Agent investigations per billing cycle, with additional investigations billed separately . Custom monitors cost $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus. Learn more in the alert webhook documentation . Read more
summary: Vercel's monitoring tool, Agent, can now check alerts before they reach your paging system. When you choose "Critical Only" for a webhook, only alerts Agent marks as serious get sent to your pager.

title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
excerpt: This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system). For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook. Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale. Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs. New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline. Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motiva
summary: Meta's ad retrieval system, Andromeda, now checks over a billion ads per second, about 100 times faster than its 2024 version, while keeping close to the accuracy of the slower ranking step. Since 2025 it has also lifted conversions on Facebook by 2.4%.

title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary
excerpt: This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib. A privacy requirement must hold as data moves through Meta’s diverse data and processing systems. Historically, supporting a new requirement meant implementing the same enforcement logic separately in each system. PrivacyLib replaces this with a common library that runs inside the clients of Meta’s data and processing systems. A system integrates with PrivacyLib once, and new privacy capabilities plug in as modules that reuse that integration. PrivacyLib performs billions of checks every second, and changes are simulated and rolled out per module. For internal AI agents, whose data access paths may not be known in advance, tool calls on supported paths carry agent context to PrivacyLib. The propagated context links each access to its session, so modules can observe data use and block operations that are not allowed. At Meta, many privacy requirements ultimately come down to the same question: Can we prove that a piece of data goes only where it is allowed? At Meta’s scale, rather than relying solely on manual privacy audits, which can go out of sync as systems change, we have developed Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) to answer this question within the infrastructure itself. PAI offers efficient and reliable first-class privacy constructs embedded in Meta’s infrastructure so that products can keep evolving quickly. In previous posts, we have covered how data understanding , data lineage , and Policy Zones (our information flow control technology) play a role in PAI. Now, we are diving deep into PrivacyLib , a common library that runs inside the clients of hundreds of our data and processing systems at the point of data access. PrivacyLib plays an important role in the final stage of the broader PAI workflow: continuously enforcing and monitoring data flows. This blog post focuses on PrivacyLib’s role in the final stage of the PAI workflow. Before PrivacyLib, we integrated privacy enforcement separately into the clients of each data and processing system for each requirement. With this approach, implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Each new requirement, whether purpose limitation or data flow discovery, needed the same set of capabilities: covering a wide range of systems; deploying in weeks rather than months; running on every data access without becoming a latency problem; and rolling out enforcement changes without taking the fleet down. Over time, this approach became harder to scale as requirements and systems evolved. PrivacyLib separates system integration from requirement implementation. We integrate each system once. When a requirement can be met at the point of data access, we implement it as a PrivacyLib module shared across the systems already integrated, so a new requirement no longer needs a separate implementation in each system. There are two kinds of modules: Enforcing modules can block a data access. For example, Policy Zones enforces purpose limitation . Observing modules only record a data access. For example, Privacy Probes collects the runtime signals used to discover data flows. As internal AI agents became a new way of accessing data, we also added the Agent Observability module to observe agent-related data access events and help safeguard the data that agents can reach. Systems already integrated with PrivacyLib picked it up without new integration work, which is what integrating once buys: each new privacy capability arrives as a module, not as a project. PrivacyLib replaces repeated implementations across systems. Engineering Challenges and Approaches of PrivacyLib at Meta’s Scale PrivacyLib operates across a broad range of data access paths at Meta: More than a hundred libraries used to access data services, from key/value stores to AI features. Thousands of production services with versions of the deployed library. Millions of assets being accessed daily. Billions of checks
summary: Meta built PrivacyLib, a shared library that runs inside its data systems and checks each data access against privacy rules. Teams now add a new privacy rule once as a module instead of rebuilding it in every system, which speeds up rollouts. It also watches what internal AI agents access.

title: Python Typing Survey 2026: AI Tools and the Shifting Checker Landscape
excerpt: The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more than one, and missing library type information was the most common difficulty. For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next. Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty. Key Takeaways From the 2026 Python Typing Survey This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities: Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks. Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them. Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work , especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward. AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs. AI Tools Now Write Types and Respond to Checker Errors The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options. Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else. Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors: “I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.” “Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.” When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. We still need empirical evidence about which interactions actually help. The Pyrefly team is already studying how AI coding tools and type checkers work together. At the 2026 Python Typing Summit, the team presented Type Checking in Agentic Workflows . Library Gaps Lead Overall; Occasional Users Struggle With Complexity Missing type information in third-party libraries was the leading difficulty, selected by 65.1% of 1,486 respondents. Another 44.6% said the type system could not describe everything their code does. Developers can still have a poor experience after a library ships dedicated stubs. Among 156 people who wrote their own answer, 22 described dynamic constructs, decorators, metaprogram
summary: Meta's 2026 survey of 1,794 Python developers found that type hint use barely changed, but many people switched or added type checker tools. The most common problem was missing type information in outside libraries, and many developers now use AI tools that write types or fix checker errors.

title: What took the Internet offline in Q3 2026
excerpt: The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet, Cloudflare Radar can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event. In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters. Disruptions at a glance Between July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq, while renewed conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region showed how quickly connectivity can become part of a broader political and humanitarian crisis. Outages within the United States, Japan, and Portugal — countries with a relatively strong history of Internet resilience — remind us that no country is immune to disruption. In total, Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 disruptions during the quarter. Government-directed shutdowns accounted for 19 incidents, including 18 exam shutdowns in Iraq. Power outages followed with 14 incidents, while natural disasters accounted for five. Power failure was a leading cause of disruptions The Internet is designed to be distributed and resilient, but that resilience still depends on electricity. When power fails, routers, mobile base stations, data centers, interconnection facilities, and the networks that connect them can fail with it. Over the past three months, that dependency was one of the clearest patterns in Radar’s disruption data. Power outages were the second-most common cause of disruptions by incident count this quarter, behind government-directed exam shutdowns. In Cuba, Internet disruptions followed the erratic patterns of an unstable power grid. Radar observed four power-related outages across the quarter, meaning connectivity was affected by grid failures at least once a month. The outages took place July 6, July 14, August 3, and a three-day blackout from September 18 to 20. The traffic volume decreases ranged from 18% on July 14 to 59% on August 3. Honduras illustrated how a localized infrastructure failure can produce national-level effects. A power failure on September 10 at an interconnection facility affected at least 11 major providers, showing how concentrated traffic exchange points can become single points of failure. The outage lasted approximately three hours, during which HTTP traffic across the country fell by 63%. Two notable exceptions were the cross-border provider Telecomunicaciones de Guatemala (AS14754) and mobile carrier Celtel (AS52262), which were unaffected. This suggests that their Honduran connectivity may rely more heavily on infrastructure outside the country. Cloudflare Radar - Traffic volume by autonomous system On July 5, a power outage in Sevastopol, Ukraine, caused an eight-hour blackout, with HTTP traffic dropping by 98%. A little over a month later, on August 12, drone strikes targeting energy infrastructure caused another power outage, resulting in a ten-hour Internet disruption and up to a 95% decline in traffic volume. As discussed in more detail below, geopolitical conflict remains a major driver of Internet disruptions. These incidents also show how conflict, energy infra
summary: Cloudflare reviewed internet outages from July to September 2026, finding 49 disruptions. Power failures were a leading cause, knocking out connections in places like Cuba, Honduras and Ukraine, and exam-related government shutdowns in Iraq were the most common overall.

title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
excerpt: Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised , creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell : serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web. Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations , updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection . As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free. Put our WAF to the test Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential. That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge , run through our Bug Bounty program . We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag. How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell . The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container , with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag . The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file. Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag . You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form. Challenge requirements This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne . All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne terms and the Cloudflare HackerOne program rules the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty: All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms before participating in the CTF. Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request. Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through the CTF user interface (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review. Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide: The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes. Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain. An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag. The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification. What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about. UI verification does not submit a HackerOne report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible. Awards require a materially distinct bypass m
summary: Cloudflare is running a time-limited hacking challenge where security researchers try to break through its firewall protections for a deliberately weak PHP website and steal a hidden file. The goal is to test defenses against two serious PHP flaws, since AI now helps attackers find new weaknesses faster.

title: Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
excerpt: Serdar Cellat , Yuchen Xie , Bernadette Marcu , Blaid Burgess , Cody Jarrett , Carlos Pereira , Qing Shi , Samuel Carvajal , Manuel Pamplona , Dorothy Jung , Feiko Ritsema , Benjamin Klein , Alex Woo , Eugene Lok , Anna Pulido , Rebecka Swe , Sanford Holsapple Introduction Clips in the Netflix mobile app. At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips , our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort. Our Video Resizing Approach Converting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot. We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead. An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios. Shot Detection and Splitting First, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles. Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop. Focus Region Discovery Once shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera. Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing. Temporal Reframing Once we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic. The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path. Tooling and Workflow Integration We integrated the resizing algorithm directly into our internal Clips tool, so editors and producers can access it as part of their existing workflow. The
summary: Netflix built an automatic tool that turns wide movie scenes into vertical and square versions for its mobile Clips feed and marketing. It finds the main characters, follows who is speaking, and moves the crop smoothly, so editors no longer reframe videos by hand.

title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
excerpt: By Praneeth Yenugutala , Victor Dusa , Anastasia Samoilova , Megan Ren , Justin Wei , Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive , an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro . It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic. Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked. To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes. Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim). Figure 1. Pensive AI architecture. Always-on error extraction and on-demand debugging complement each other and share log sources, the LLM gateway, tracing, and the cache. Archived logs feed offline evals and release gates. The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough. Part 1: Finding the useful errors Legacy Pensive rules are precise, but each one captures a particular log shape. A simplified rule looks like this: - name: SparkContainerOOM logSource: GENIE_STDERR restartable: false regex: "Container.*is running beyond physical memory limits.*Killing container" summary: Spark AM container runs out of memory With Pensive AI, we wanted to find useful errors that had no correspond
summary: Netflix built Pensive AI, which uses AI to read logs from failed data jobs and point out the likely cause. Before, its rule-based system left about half of failures unexplained; now AI extraction covers every failure.

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. What happened GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions. Immediate remediation After disabling the model , we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it: To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised. To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Rely
summary: Cloudflare found that its GLM-5.3 AI model sometimes sent very long requests' replies containing bits of other customers' data, from August 27 to September 9, 2026. About 155 replies were affected, and they fixed the problem by correcting the model's memory setup and patching the software.

title: AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)
excerpt: A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice. Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo. The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future. The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon). Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer. The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge. Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week. Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine n
summary: AWS launched Continuum, a service that finds code security flaws, proves which ones can be exploited, and opens fixes for a person to approve. It also released Amazon ECS Gateway, which lets network teams and app teams share how services are exposed, at no extra charge.
