title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
excerpt: By Roberto Perez Alcolea , Java Platform Team Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it. Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves. Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next: Does any consumer still call this method? Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations? Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact? Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign? At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds. Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally. We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions: What changed in the library’s public API? Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed? The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing. From API Changes to Consumer Impact Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive. Quasar builds on SCIP , an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently. On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change. During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings

title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management
excerpt: Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography. While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography . Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later. For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work. The evolution of GeoKey Manager Cloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security ( TLS ) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager . This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network. GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key. That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel . This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries. Global ciphertext, regional key unwrapping In its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used from and when. Separate workstreams determine where tunnels terminate, where traffic is inspected, how it is routed, and where plaintext processing occurs. But all
summary: Cloudflare has launched a closed beta of a new key manager that keeps customers' decryption keys usable only in their chosen region, and it uses encryption designed to resist future quantum computers. This helps organizations meet local data-location rules while protecting sensitive data that must stay secret for years.

title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
excerpt: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale. So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%. Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests , a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule , and Cloudflare handles the rest. A request for part of a file An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header: GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range : HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576 Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it. The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it. The range-size problem Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration. The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post : each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone. The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key. This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming , a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range. The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology. Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently. Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora -based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers. Fixed-size cache chunks The fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache
summary: Cloudflare rebuilt how its cache handles partial file requests, like video seeking, so it no longer pulls large extra chunks from the origin. The new Origin Range Requests feature is available on all plans, needs no size tuning, and is turned on with a Cache Rule.

title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
excerpt: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host. We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched. The cost of good neighbors Multi-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management. These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota. A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota. We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. And Mount Mayhem traced container-startup slowness to a global kernel lock amplified by modern CPU cache topology. Each of these raised t
summary: Netflix added a mode to its container platform, Titus, that gives sensitive workloads their own virtual machine instead of sharing a host with other teams. It keeps the same tools and managed setup, and is meant to stop other containers from slowing down the most demanding real-time services.

title: Localizing compliance at scale: achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
excerpt: For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework . For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators. What a Korean user sees when they sign up The most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: " By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy. " A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once: 모두 동의 (Agree to all) [필수] 서비스 약관 ([Required] Terms of Service) [필수] 개인정보 수집 및 이용 ([Required] Collection and use of personal information) [필수] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 해외 이전 ([Required] Transfer of a limited amount of personal information overseas) [선택] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 제3자 제공 ([Optional] Sharing a limited amount of personal information with marketing third parties) The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications). The hard part: sign-up paths that never show a form Itemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely. Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change. We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflare’s sign-up form, which enforces the required consents. The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountry header at the origin and as request.cf.country inside a Worker. Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison: // Illustrative: the shape of the check, not Cloudflare's own dashboard code. export default { async fetch(request) { // Two-letter country code derived from the client IP. // Same value as the CF-IPCountry request header. // Cloudflare's network populates this on the incoming request, so there is // no geolocation database, lookup service, or extra round trip of our own. const country = request.cf?.country; if (country === "KR") { return renderSignUp({ locale: "ko-KR", consent: "itemized", // four separate items, three of them required socialLogin: false,
summary: Cloudflare received South Korea's ISMS-P security certification after ten days of audits by Korean regulators. For Korean users, sign-up now shows separately labeled consent items, and social login is turned off there so every account passes through that form.

title: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available
excerpt: Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities . AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define. Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes. Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems. Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path. For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in action To show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities . Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S
summary: AWS has released AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities to general availability. It finds security flaws in your code, checks which ones are actually exploitable in your setup, and proposes a fix as a pull request that a person must approve before anything ships.

excerpt: Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: Minimize coordination Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the architecture once it arrived. Git operations are a Tier 0 service: they’re a core function of GitHub, and nearly everything in GitHub depends on the repository data. That meant the data, services, and every dependency had to move first. The first copy of a repository landed in Azure’s Central US region in August 2025. Today, most repositories have two of their five replicas in Azure, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. For most of that time, Azure absorbed our growth while our own data centers held steady. During the migration, traffic follows the data. Most repositories have five replicas to balance durability, availability, and scale. To minimize read latency, Spokes uses preferential routing to direct traffic to a replica in the same region and availability zone as the request. As replicas move to Azure, the share of the traffic that can be served from Azure grows with each one, until the last replica arrives and the old region stops receiving requests entirely. Every repository goes through this process: No repository left behind So, what about the remaining 0.00001% of repositories? In our current architecture, a repository hosted in more than one region has a lower write throughput ceiling. Spokes’ quorum only needs a majority to commit a write, but it waits for every healthy replica to respond (up to a timeout) before moving on, so slow replicas delay every write rather than falling behind. In practice, that means the slowest healthy replica sets the latency of every write, and because each write holds a repository-wide lock until it commits, it also sets the throughput ceiling. Once a replica lives in the target Azure region, it’s about 1,000 miles from our data centers, making each network round trip around 25ms, and a write requires multiple round trips. A repository already near its throughput ceiling can’t absorb that on every serialized write; it would fall further behind with every push. This is where our first principle, minimizing coordination, comes into play. Specifically for this case: don’t serialize what doesn’t need to be. Git’s consistency requirements apply to each reference individually. Once the server accepts an update to a reference, no client should see an older value afterward, only that value or a newer one. That holds whether the update is a fast-forward, a force push, or a delete. But in most cases, updates to different references don’t depend on each other and can be applied independently. So, we’re changing the scope of th
summary: GitHub is moving most of its busiest code repositories into Microsoft Azure, which now serves about half of Git traffic. The team also changed how writes are handled, so repositories with far-apart copies can keep up with heavy use.

title: How Commerce.com and Cloudflare are getting storefronts ready for AI agents
excerpt: AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online. That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it. Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like search_products . Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, it’s currently available behind experimental Chrome flags ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like Cloudflare Kitesurf . In August, we launched edge implementation of WebMCP in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code. Commerce.com , a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. So when the preview came out, they asked: Can we turn this on for all of our stores at once? Here’s why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP, how we built edge-level opt-outs to give every merchant control, and what we learned along the way. Why Commerce.com wanted WebMCP Kristina Pototska, Product Management Director at Commerce.com, explains why this matters for storefronts: “Merchants keep asking us how they can keep up with agentic shopping. When a shopper asks an agent to find something, merchants want their store to be in the answer. They want to keep the customer, keep control of the checkout, and do it without rebuilding their site. WebMCP helps with all three. The agent gets real tools to search products, check details, build a cart, and get a checkout link, so it doesn’t have to guess its way around the page. The human shopper stays on the merchant’s site, and the merchant keeps the relationship. We wanted to turn this on in a secure way, and without asking merchants to edit their theme or do anything by hand. That’s where the Cloudflare partnership worked perfectly. WebMCP also works side by side with our server-side MCP , and together they cover the different ways people shop with agents. Server-side MCP supports agents that connect to a store directly, like an assistant helping someone shop across several sites. WebMCP supports agents that work in the shopper’s browser. It’s the same set of shopping tools in both cases, so merchants don’t have to choose between the two or manage them separately.” Under the hood, this integration relies on two key principles. First, the WebMCP tools execute directly inside the shopper's active browser session on the storefront's domain, ensuring the agent sees the same prices and cart. No credentials go to a third party, and the visit still happens on the merchant's site. Second, Cloudflare serves as the edge delivery layer for Commerce.com’s backend MCP server, proxying tool definitions and actions unchanged so merchants maintain full control over their tool logic. What a shopper's agent sees When visiting an enabled Commerce.com storefront, an AI assistant no longer has to guess how to navigate the site. Instead, it can instantly discover tools via WebMCP. Suppose you tell your agent: "Find me a waterproof trail running shoe under $140 in size 10 and add it to my cart." Without WebMCP: The agent attempts to simulate human clicks, only to get blocked by cookie banners, misinterpret variant drop-downs, or get tripped up by bot challenges that try to distinguish automated traffic from real customers. With WebMCP: The agent detects the store's tools on document.modelContext and makes two
summary: Cloudflare and Commerce.com now let AI shopping agents use online stores through built-in tools, instead of clicking around pages. Stores can turn this on without writing code, so agents can find products and add items to carts more reliably.

title: Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability
excerpt: Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release. All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed session.upload_progress.name are not covered by the WAF rule. The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability. More information to follow. October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell . The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic. Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation , OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell. Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic. Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives. To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability. Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog . The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users. What we know about the vulnerabilities PHP is used by almost 70% of websites . The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet. The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released. An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large r
summary: Security researchers found two serious flaws in PHP, a popular web language, that could let attackers run harmful code on servers. Cloudflare rolled out automatic protections for its customers about nine hours before the public announcement, and says patching PHP is still needed.

title: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF
excerpt: Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester. These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper. Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error. With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability. And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans. Request inspection is not enough Cloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin. For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server. The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction. As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory: GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence: 200 OK Content-Type: text/plain [database] username=app_service password=EXAMPLE_SECRET Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentat
summary: Cloudflare is adding a feature to its web firewall that checks both the incoming request and the server's reply together. It can spot when an attack worked, like a leaked password, and block that reply before it reaches the attacker. This is available to all customers, including free plans.

title: Introducing tsrs: A port of TypeScript to Rust
excerpt: Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs , a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain . Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser. To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that. The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like. Performance and memory improvements Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers: As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs , and we’re hoping to find more. You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration. By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster: Try tsrs TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm: npm install tsrs npx tsrs Why now? We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go. However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript. Why Rust? You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?” However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly . The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency. Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run ful
summary: Cloudflare, VoidZero, and Owner.com are building tsrs, a version of the TypeScript code checker rewritten in Rust, working with the TypeScript team. Early tests show it can run up to 8 times faster and use about 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0.

title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
excerpt: On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet. We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services. We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected. Our response We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms. Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below. What customers should do Developer guidance For developers, look beneath the SDK. An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy. Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore. This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment. Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier. Timeline The timeline of events so far is below. Date and Time Event October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment. October 20, 02:00 UTC Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms. October 20 09:15 UTC Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published. O
summary: Cloudflare found that private keys for eight eMudhra certificates, which browsers and systems widely trust, were stolen. Attackers could use them to fake secure websites, so Cloudflare patched its services and says it found no active abuse of its own systems.

title: Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services
excerpt: When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs) , AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization. Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway , a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account. ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams. Platform teams create and configure a gateway, defining organizational networking standards including subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and WAF web ACLs, in a single place. They then associate the gateway with one or more ECS clusters, making it available to services running on those clusters. Application teams opt their services in by adding a gateway connector parameter when creating or updating a service. ECS provisions the required per-service resources automatically: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, target groups, and a service security group that permits inbound traffic only from the ALB. No networking expertise required. ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes. A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console , platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later. Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings , you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation. Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector. aws ecs create-gateway \ --name my-team-gateway \ --infrastructure-role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ECSGatewayRole \ --configuration '{ "HostSharedAlb": { "networkConfiguration": { "subnets": [ "subnet-080779f9bd887757a", "subnet-03d5b2fead6bc6258", "subnet-0861210a397d31252", "subnet-06539e194023cb77a" ], "ipAddressType": "ipv4" }, "scheme": "internet-facing" } }' Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters. Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters. Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster: aws ecs associate-gateway-with-cluster \ --gateway my-team-gateway \ --cluster arn:aws:ecs:us-e
summary: Amazon announced ECS Gateway, which automatically sets up the network pieces needed to reach containerized apps on Amazon ECS. Platform teams define standard settings once, and each new service gets its own web address and security setup without manual work.

title: Introducing ModuleLens: Zooming into PyTorch Modules for Human and Agentic Engineering
excerpt: Lida Li, Sr. Staff Software Engineer, Product ML Infra Introduction Modern recommendation systems, including those used for ads ranking and content discovery, have grown substantially in scale and complexity. This growth stems from both increasingly large model architectures. The resulting memory footprint often exceeds the capacity of a single GPU, making it necessary to shard production models across multiple GPUs using distributed training techniques such as Distributed Model Parallelism (DMP). This evolution brings challenges to the everyday engineer work on testing and debugging the model code. The bottleneck includes: Local Machine Hardware Limits : Because production models require multi-GPU setups, initializing a full model locally on a single-gpu workstation is virtually impossible. Input Data Dependencies : When an engineer modifies code inside a specific downstream module, getting realistic input data is a major hurdle. Traditionally, obtaining that input requires initializing the entire multi-GPU pipeline from scratch and executing every preceding module in the network — wasting immense amounts of time and computation resources. Slow Iteration Feedback Loops : Engineers face prolonged iteration loops when attempting to verify sub-module changes, as every code edit requires re-executing or re-initializing heavy distributed trainer setups. To eliminate these bottlenecks, we build ModuleLens , which pivots from a legacy “Model-First” paradigm to an isolated “Module-First” engineering framework. The following table contrasts these two operational paradigms across key engineering metrics: Under the module-first paradigm, engineers can isolate any given module, avoid multi-GPU model initialization entirely, and reconstruct and profile it locally within seconds. In addition to accelerating developer workflows, this modular foundation offers a fast, structured execution environment that empowers autonomous AI agents to analyze, refactor, and optimize PyTorch code independently. Architecture The architecture of ModuleLens is organized into three primary components: ModuleTracer for capturing runtime data, Module Repo for central storage, and a Consumption Layer serving human interfaces and AI-based tooling. The following diagram depicts this structure. ModuleTracer ModuleTracer is designed to capture and record all essential data — including input and output tensors, model parameter weights, and initialization arguments. This comprehensive tracking allows any target PyTorch module to be reconstructed seamlessly within the consumption layer, enabling offline execution with captured inputs and validation against expected outputs. To carry out trace capture, ModuleTracer relies on several key mechanisms: Non-Intrusive PyTorch Forward Hooks: Attaches listeners directly to PyTorch modules to seamlessly log parameter weights (state_dict), input and output tensors, and execution metadata during runtime. In-Memory Module Init Tracking: Ensures target modules can be reconstructed by dynamically tracking initialization arguments (__init__ args and kwargs). It achieves this in memory by inspecting imported classes and patching Python’s __import__ function. Resource-Efficient Tracing Loops: Reduces GPU compute overhead by registering early_stop_func and post_train_step_func callbacks. These wait for model warmup, capture data across a single training step, and terminate early. Optimized Handling of Large Tensors: To efficiently profile large tensors, ModuleTracer automatically enables shape-only tracing (log_shapes), logging solely tensor dimensions so that synthetic inputs can be reconstructed during restoration. Additionally, if an input tensor is shared across multiple modules, ModuleTracer retains only a single copy and uses reference links for all other instances. ModuleRepo Extracted module state is persisted within a queryable backend built on top of the Weights & Biases (WandB) Registry. All captured modules are stored into one
summary: Pinterest built ModuleLens, a tool that records the inputs and settings of one piece of a large AI model so engineers can test and debug it alone on a single machine. This avoids running the full multi-GPU model each time, saving time and compute. It also lets automated AI helpers work on the code.

title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
excerpt: Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning. We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents. We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. The Problem: More Context, Worse Results Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. The Approach: A Thin Router With Specialist Workers We split the system into two layers: A deterministic orchestrator that performs zero domain work. It classifies intent, gathers required fields, runs reliability checks, and delegates to the right specialist. It never reasons about code, never generates configurations, and never touches the codebase. It’s a router. Fourteen specialized subagents , each a complete domain expert with isolated context. A schema management agent knows configuration registries. A population agent knows how to generate code for each of 10 data sources. A validation agent knows build systems and quality checks. No agent sees the full picture. That’s the feature, not the bug. The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Read the relevant subagent’s instruction file. Check if the target already exists (prevent duplicates). Gather required fields from the user. Auto-discover what can be inferred (repository type, existing configurations). Reliability gate check for active warnings or required rev
summary: Meta built a small controller for its AI agents that only routes tasks and runs safety checks, while 14 specialist agents handle the actual work. A single do-everything agent had started making mistakes in production, and this split made the system more accurate and efficient.

title: GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary
excerpt: Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world knowledge built into LLMs makes ad matching more intelligent and precise, compounding gains for advertisers. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Rather than maintaining a dedicated ID for every item, GenRecs Tokenization represents each item with a set of tokens from a stable semantic vocabulary. Paired with Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) and Meta’s Adaptive Ranking Model , GenRecs Tokenization has delivered a +0.35% lift in conversions across surfaces for advertisers. GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders , GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal. GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases: Accelerating learning from new entities: Semantic tokenization helps models to infer relevance and establish relationships through shared concepts. New entities include newly created ads, niche products, and pages with limited engagement. Enabling cross-campaign transfer: Semantic tokenization creates a stable vocabulary that allows the models to carry insights across campaigns for advertisers. LLM scaling benefits: Semantic tokenization allows the benefits to compound with the LLM scaling curve’s improving performance. Infusing world knowledge: Semantic tokenization gives pre-trained language models a direct interface to reason about ad content and user intent. Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields: Prediction accuracy improvements in production: Paired with Meta’s GEM and Adaptive Ranking Model , GenRecs Tokenization delivered a +0.35% lift 1 in conversions. Compounding feedback loop: Better tail predictions yield better lessons from tail ads which enrich the training data to further improve predictions for all ads from the model, creating a performance improving feedback loop. A new way to scale: Across production ranking and retrieval, tokens bend the scaling curve along sequence length, training data, and model architecture. 1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026. summary: Meta describes a new way to pick ads for people, using language-model style 'tokens' that describe what each ad is about instead of a fixed ID per ad. This helps the system guess well for brand-new products with no history, and it lifted advertiser conversions by 0.35% in Meta's own tests.

title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
excerpt: With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible. The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise ~1 million GPUs. Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently. Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people. Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models , including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it. Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind. https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_Video_v1.mp4 The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center. The Supercluster: Unlocking New AI Capabilities Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine. This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep. Multiple Generations of AI Hardware Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 ) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric. Catalina: NVIDIA GB200 Our first platform, Catalina , leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100 . It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP) . The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. We chose Ariel because the GB200 NVL72 scaled up nearly every other dimension relative to the NVIDIA H100: FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, scale-up bandwidth, and scale-up domain size, while scale-out bandwidth per GPU would have stayed at 400G. We ex
summary: Meta has finished the first phase of Prometheus, a huge AI computing system in Ohio with hundreds of thousands of chips, and plans to grow it to about one million. It was used to train Meta's new Muse AI models.
