title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
excerpt: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update. If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls. This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server? Citrix released software updates to address the flaw , and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch. Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth , to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue. Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform. The NetScaler exploit Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks. CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771 . In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the
summary: A serious flaw in Citrix NetScaler gateways let attackers run commands without logging in, and it is being actively exploited. The post urges fast patching, plus extra layers like access limits and firewall rules to guard login pages against future flaws.

title: Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
excerpt: When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April , an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave. Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before. About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in. How a review doubled in cost The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data. The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though. At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models. Our internal standards reviewer, Codex , ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself. The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost. What else has changed since our last post? One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable . We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out! So, where were the tokens going? Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%, cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again. That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the contex
summary: Cloudflare's AI code reviewer cost rose to about $2.46 per review by August, so they worked to cut it. Through tuning the reviewer's code and switching which AI models it uses, they lowered the average cost to $0.77 and made reviews faster.

title: Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models
excerpt: Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs. Context When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow , a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows. We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models. Introducing System One extraction models Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it. Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds. An extraction model can return: Extracted values: Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score. Including, computed values: Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score. Estimated values: Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval. Forecasted values: Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval. And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look. He
summary: Cloudflare announced a preview of Clairic, a fast, cheap AI model that pulls names, dates, and numbers out of messy text and makes estimates, without writing out long answers. It is available now on their platform, and they plan to release it openly soon.

title: AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Lambda Web Functions, Amazon S3 on the Vercel Marketplace, and more (October 19, 2026)
excerpt: Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction. The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines AWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy , and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code. Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control. The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel – You can now provision S3 general purpose buckets, S3 Tables , and S3 Vectors from the Vercel dashboard, or by describing what you want to build in v0. It joins existing integrations for Amazon Aurora , Amazon DynamoDB , and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , so the whole stack sits in one AWS account with one bill. The authentication detail is the good part: a short-lived OIDC token is exchanged at runtime with AWS Security Token Service for credentials scoped to that resource, so no static keys are stored anywhere. Amazon EC2 T8i instances are now available in South America (São Paulo) – The newest burstable generation reached the São Paulo Region, which matters for the unglamorous half of a workload: login gateways, small database
summary: AWS Lambda can now run ordinary web apps directly, with no rewrite and no adapter, and you get a live web address in under a minute. Amazon S3 storage can also be set up from Vercel, a web-building tool, without opening the AWS console.

title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
excerpt: Prasanna Vijayanathan , Renzo Sanchez-Silva When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded. This post is about that search for the needle. The Four hours before a fix Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it? As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner. The MELT Layer “What caused the issue?” Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to. MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system. The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer: What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves out The timeline of an investigation So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again? A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hours In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover. The disagreement underneath The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow. It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle. Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas , our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found. The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differin
summary: Netflix describes how investigating a slowdown can take about four hours, mostly spent piecing together how its many monitoring and alert tools relate to each other. They propose a shared map of these connections, called an ontology or knowledge graph, so engineers and AI helpers can find the cause faster.

title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
excerpt: A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug. As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria: Identify yourself accurately and securely Do only what you say you will do Don’t engage in abusive behavior Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm . Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.” This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important: Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next. Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior. For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked. Do not engage in abusive behavior This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences , that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust. We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are: Does the bot respect instructions? Did it respond to direct feedback? We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar , as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify. When in Rome, do as the Romans do A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time. Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309 . And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals. What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (“Too Many Requests”) response. A 429 is a directive for
summary: Cloudflare is adding a system that scores how well its approved 'verified' bots respect website owners' rules, such as robots.txt and requests to slow down. Scores will be shown publicly on Cloudflare Radar, so bots that ignore site rules lose trust over time.

title: Staying Evergreen: How we automated secure access and repo hygiene in a shared org
excerpt: Working with outside collaborators can add more work for a repository owner. You need to confirm who still needs access, change permissions as projects evolve, and archive repositories once they’ve served their purpose. To keep up, repository owners need to track collaborators, deadlines, and follow-ups for each repository. As a project grows, that manual housekeeping becomes harder to keep up with and easier to defer. We faced this problem in a shared organization where GitHub employees (“Hubbers”) collaborate with customers and partners on product trials and professional services engagements. Our answer was Evergreen , a GitHub App built with native GitHub features. The workflows below exhibit a pattern you can adapt for your own organization. Meet Evergreen Evergreen is a GitHub App that automates organization hygiene through two workflows: Outside collaborator access reviews. Every quarter, each repo’s outside collaborators are reviewed. Keep who you need, and everyone else is removed. Stale repository detection and archival. Repos with no human activity past a threshold get flagged, warned, and (if still untouched) archived. Two design principles shaped everything: Fail secure. If nobody responds to an access review, we don’t leave access in place and hope for the best. We revoke it. The safe outcome is the default outcome. Never destroy anything. Evergreen will never delete a repository or its contents. Archived repos are recoverable, and every access change is written into the repo’s tracking issue, so reverting a mistake is as easy as a copy-paste to Copilot. How it works: One brain, many hands Under the hood, Evergreen is a small Go webhook server running in a container. But the interesting part is the choreography . Every moving piece is a stock GitHub feature: a GitHub App, scheduled actions, webhooks, issues, custom properties, and plain files in a repo. Nothing exotic to reinvent. A controller that keeps time A dedicated controller repo acts as Evergreen’s clock and its memory. Four scheduled GitHub Actions workflows fire repository_dispatch events on a quarterly cadence, and the app wakes up and does the work: Day Workflow What happens 1st Stale repo review Flag repos with no recent human activity, open a warning issue 8th Access review Snapshot outside collaborators, open a checklist issue per repo 16th Stale repo cleanup Archive repos still stale after the grace period 23rd Access cleanup Auto‑revoke access for any review left unanswered Reviews open two weeks before their cleanup runs, and there’s a hard grace period baked in so a stray manual run can never fast‑forward the guillotine. Each workflow also supports workflow_dispatch , so we can trigger any step by hand as needed. State you can git blame Evergreen tracks every repo’s status as a JSON file (one per repository) committed to the controller repo under state/repos/<repo_id>.json . The snapshot of who had access, when the review opened, the deadline, who decided, and what happened all lives there. Here’s a completed review where a Hubber kept Alice’s access and let Bob’s lapse: { "repo_id": 123456789, "full_name": "the-org/acme-trial", "last_seen_at": "2026-04-13T00:05:00Z", "access_review": { "deadline": "2026-04-27T00:00:00Z", "status": "renewed", "collaborators_at_open": [ { "login": "alice", "name": "Alice Example", "permission": "admin" }, { "login": "bob", "name": "Bob Example", "permission": "write" } ], "renewed_logins": ["alice"], "decided_by": "carol-hubber", "decided_at": "2026-04-15T16:42:10Z", "tracking_issue": { "repo_id": 123456789, "number": 42 } }, "staleness": { "last_activity_at": "2026-04-15T16:42:10Z", "warned_at": null, "archive_deadline": null, "status": "active", "tracking_issue": null } } The best part: because state is just files in git, the commit history is the audit trail. Want to know why someone lost access last spring? git log the state file. There’s no separate database or bespoke audit pipeline to track. Issue‑ops, eve

title: 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale
excerpt: Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record! There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time. Some highlights: WhatsApp: More than 30 million messages per second during the July 19 final (Argentina vs. Spain), 1.23x the peak of New Year’s Eve 2026 and an all-time platform record. The previous record had already fallen 12 days earlier, during the Round of 16 match between Argentina and Egypt, at 29 million messages per second. Messenger, Threads, and Instagram Direct: 49 million messages per minute at peak. Instagram: Recommendation system traffic up to 80% higher week-over-week. Final-squad players collectively added +213.6 million activated followers — a 6.6% increase — with combined followings surging from 3.26 billion to 3.47 billion. Live video: Watch time spiked +90% on Instagram and +242% on Facebook, versus the July baseline. Threads : 1.5 billion impressions on tournament-tagged posts, reaching about 15 million people daily and peaking at 25 million on July 6. Facebook : 80 million posts mentioning the World Cup. Traffic Followed the Breaks, Not the Ball Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle. But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament. It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel. Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern. Layered Systems, No Manual Intervention Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand. Region-Specific Capacity Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament. Instagram: Preparing for 39 Consecutive Days of Surges For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience. During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours. Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final. Capacity buffers: Our products went into the tournament with sufficient capacity, which meant real buffers were available to allocate. We pre-provisioned significant additional capacity across all serving tiers so that spikes never had to wait on autoscaling to catch up. These dedicated buffers were our single most effective lever of the tournament. Country-level graceful degradation: For high-risk matches, we shed non-critical background load in the top-traffic nations (Brazil, Argentina, India, Indonesia, Spain) to protect core functionality. title: How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering
excerpt: Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups. To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the development cycle. We’re sharing insights into what it took to build Forum with agentic AI: how we adapted the codebase, tested frameworks and internal tooling for agentic execution, what worked, and what didn’t. Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type. That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review. From Human-In-The-Loop to Human-On-The-Loop Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step. With human-in-the-loop , the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it. With human-on-the-loop , the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration. When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t. So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change. With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible: Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike. Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers. title: Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award
excerpt: Ke Mao, Mark Harman, and Yue Jia have been recognized with the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis ( ISSTA) 2026 Most Influential Paper Award for their 2016 research, “ Sapienz: multi-objective automated testing for Android applications. ” The recognition celebrates a decade of impact from work that began at University College London and went on to become testing infrastructure at Meta. Sapienz automatically tests apps to find crashes and helps engineers reproduce them in fewer steps, making failures easier to investigate. The original research combined three goals: exploring more of an app, finding more crashes, and reducing the number of steps needed to trigger them. In its evaluation on 1,000 popular Google Play apps, Sapienz found 558 previously unknown crashes. Within 17 months of publication, Sapienz was deployed at scale at Meta. Today, it runs millions of tests daily across Meta’s platforms, surfaces thousands of unique crashes each week, and helps safeguard hundreds of app releases each month, supporting product reliability and quality. Sapienz’s applications quickly expanded beyond crash detection. By using test accounts with synthetic conversations, it became the app-exploration engine for dynamic taint analysis at WhatsApp. We shared Sapienz’s journey in October in our ISSTA 2026 keynote delivered by Ke Mao, “Finding the Bugs Users Would Find: From Sapienz to Autonomous Agents.” Beyond detecting crashes, large language model (LLM) agents can now explore apps and reason about whether their behavior matches what users should expect, extending automated testing from reliability to functional correctness and, increasingly, automated repair. Sapienz’s core ideas of multi-objective exploration and actionable fault revelation carry over directly. A decade on, those founding principles still hold true. As part of Meta’s overall privacy and risk management program, this work reflects our ongoing efforts to ensure privacy considerations are at the heart of our product development process, helping teams identify risks earlier in the development lifecycle, apply safeguards more consistently, and build privacy protections into each new innovation from the start. title: A fully programmable secure web gateway
excerpt: Every secure web gateway on the market works the same way: traffic matches a condition. A terminal action fires. Allow, Block, Isolate, Log. This model has been the foundation of network security for nearly 30 years, and it handles the common case well. But it has a ceiling, and customers with complex environments hit that ceiling regularly. Earlier this year, we shared our vision to build a truly programmable SASE platform . We also outlined how the term programmability has become diluted by the security industry. Most vendors claim programmability because they have public APIs, Terraform providers, webhooks, and alerting. Cloudflare offers all of those things too, but that’s not enough. True programmability means running your own code — arbitrary logic that you wrote for your specific environment — inline in the policy evaluation path, at the moment a security decision is made. Today, we’re excited to announce Cloudflare is bringing true programmability to Cloudflare Gateway and DLP (Data Loss Prevention) by integrating it with the entirety of our edge computing platform. We are releasing a new type of Gateway action, Forward , and custom validation functions, available to all Zero Trust plans. These capabilities allow you to use a Cloudflare Worker to transform and manipulate traffic, or to bring your own data to policy evaluation. The trade-off that every security team faces For as long as firewalls have existed, businesses have faced a binary choice. You can maintain your own security detection engine — your own firewall, your own proxy infrastructure — with high maintenance overhead and low portability, in exchange for maximum customization. Or, you can accept the constraints of a vendor, offloading the considerable maintenance cost, at the expense of flexibility to solve problems specific to your environment. In six years of building Cloudflare Gateway, we have heard from thousands of customers struggling with this trade-off. A security team migrating access controls for a critical internal application needs to inject HTTP headers based on JSON Web Token (JWT) claims from their identity provider. The data exists in the request context, but Gateway cannot read the JWT and write the header. So the team stands up a pool of NGINX proxies solely to perform this transformation. That infrastructure now must be patched, monitored, and secured... indefinitely. Another team wants a Slack notification the moment an employee signs up for a new SaaS service. The policy engine can detect the sign-up event, but it can only Allow or Block. So the team builds a Logpush-to-SIEM-to-Slack pipeline with a 5 to 15 minute delay and no guarantee of delivery. And piles on yet another piece of infrastructure. Dozens of enterprise customers have asked for warning pages that prompt users for justification before allowing access to sensitive destinations. Most then want to customize the ensuing behavior based on additional context about who the user is and the level of access requested. But serving customized, dynamic responses from a policy engine is exceedingly difficult. We have offered customers many extension points over the years. But along with every other firewall vendor, it is impossible to build features to cover threat vectors as quickly as they can appear. However, we also recognize that the best solutions are those which are infinitely extensible to your environment. Why only Cloudflare can solve this problem Cloudflare is not just a firewall, or a secure web gateway, a content delivery network, or an edge service. Cloudflare is a composable compute platform. Cloudflare Workers already allows customers to run complex logic on our network edge from any of our 330+ locations worldwide. Cloudflare Gateway already evaluates and enforces security policy on user traffic at those same locations, on the same machines, in the same data centers. title: Deploy with Void
excerpt: VoidZero's tools such as Vite, Vitest, Oxc, and Rolldown — bundled in one toolchain as Vite+ — have made frontend development faster, but building full-stack applications requires more than just a tooling stack. These applications need server routes, databases, local development environments, and a fast and easy way to deploy ideas to production. We’re excited to open-source three new products that bring server routing, typed data access, and Cloudflare deployment into a unified Vite workflow. Void Platform: A shared deployment platform for teams to host Void apps on Cloudflare. Void SDK: A composable JavaScript SDK for building full-stack apps with Vite. Void CLI: A CLI for provisioning resources and deploying Vite apps to Cloudflare. The CLI deploys apps built with the SDK to the Platform. All three products are open-sourced as a single JavaScript package and Vite plugin that you can install via npm install void . With Void , you can build your server and client together, carry types from your database to the UI, and let Void automatically provision the Cloudflare resources that your app uses. We originally set out to build a single, private platform for all users to deploy apps to. After VoidZero joined Cloudflare , we adjusted our direction to open-source the platform and allow anyone to install because we saw a growing need: companies want to encourage vibe-coded internal apps, but are concerned about security and do not want to give cloud access to every employee . Void addresses this problem. Void Platform: a cloud platform for your company The Void Platform is fully open source and you can fork it and adapt it to your needs by integrating your company's systems, customize deployment workflows, build features for your customers, or make it work on other deployment platforms. Use the platform as it is, contribute improvements upstream, or fork it and build only the features you need. The open source code can be used out of the box or as a starting point. As an admin of a Void Platform, you control access, set resource limits, inspect deployments and usage through the Void CLI or admin dashboard, and provide guardrails so everyone else can ship serious and vibe coded apps to the same shared platform. By installing a Void Platform, your team or customers have a shared deployment environment in your Cloudflare account on top of Workers for Platforms . Void Platform enables: Faster prototyping . Your team can quickly build prototypes, deploy them, and share working apps for feedback, without setting up a separate Cloudflare account or provisioning resources for every project. This reduces the time to ship internal apps from days/weeks to minutes. Non-technical teams building . This workflow also lets teammates who do not normally write code work with coding agents to build and share their own apps. A designer can create an interactive prototype, or an operations teammate can build an internal dashboard, then deploy it to the same platform. All with the right security measures in place. To self-host a Void platform, you need: A Cloudflare account with Workers for Platforms and R2 enabled A PostgreSQL database An account with your chosen login provider A domain for your apps Then install Void as a cloud platform by running a single command: Once your platform is set up, approved users can connect to it via the Void CLI for deployment. void connect https://api.orange-company.dev A user builds their app using the Void SDK, which is what powers Void Platform benefits like authentication, framework detection, resource provisioning, and more. In other words, Void Platform only works because of the accompanying SDK and CLI. title: TimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads
excerpt: By Oleksii Tkachuk , Rajiv Shringi , Chris Lohfink , Abe Ratnofsky , Kartik Sathyanarayanan Introduction In an earlier post , we introduced the TimeSeries Abstraction, our high-throughput, low-latency platform designed to store and query temporal event data at scale. It has since become the operational backbone for Netflix’s largest datasets, which now span multiple petabytes. However, managing such large datasets in hot storage, tuned for low-millisecond latency access , is not cheap. At Netflix, cost-efficiency is a continuous discipline rather than a temporary initiative. This post shares two solutions that significantly reduce storage costs by continuously moving older, less frequently accessed data into cheaper object storage: Solution 1 : Uses Apache Kafka and Flink to stream data directly to S3 Solution 2 : Leverages Cassandra backups in S3 and pluggable Memtables to read data directly from S3 We’ll start with the Kafka/Flink-based design, then describe how we evolved to a native Cassandra-based cold tier. Challenges As Netflix’s TimeSeries datasets have expanded, we’ve encountered several compounding challenges: Growing retention demands : Users often push for increasing data retention to serve a broader range of use cases, which in turn increases the storage costs. Escalating costs : Maintaining massive, dense clusters for infrequently accessed historical data is prohibitively expensive. Sparse historical access: Most queries target recent events, but older data must remain readily available for occasional audits and investigations. Operational strain : High storage density on hot nodes complicates scaling, deployment, and cluster stability. Latency requirements : Even historical data sometimes requires sub-second query performance for internal tooling and analysis. This creates a clear opportunity: keep the most recent data on fast storage and migrate older, rarely read data to cheaper storage while preserving a consistent API . Done well, this can meet user and operational needs while greatly reducing our infrastructure spend. TimeSeries Abstraction Before we dive into the cold storage solutions, here is a quick recap of how TimeSeries partitions its dataset into multiple tables, each covering a window of time we call Time Slices . Time Slices and Immutable Windows This enables several key optimizations, most notably allowing a table to become immutable once it crosses the write boundary, which lets us safely apply further optimizations. For more details, refer to our previous post . This slice information is critical and is maintained in a dedicated metadata table: Time Slice Metadata Storage Creating new Time Slices and maintaining their metadata is a primary responsibility of the TimeSeries control plane. The TimeSeries data plane uses this information to correctly route the read and write traffic to the provisioned tables. TimeSeries Data and Control Plane With that background, let’s look at the different solutions we built for data tiering. Solution 1: Streaming with Apache Kafka and Flink Our first solution followed a familiar streaming pattern using Apache Kafka and Flink, where we streamed data to S3 in realtime while simultaneously persisting it to Cassandra. Streaming with Apache Kafka and Flink Getting Data Into S3 Efficiently To optimize data streaming to S3, the system hash-partitions Time Series IDs into buckets. This partitions the stream and lets dedicated Flink tasks handle each bucket, ultimately batching and reducing the write throughput to S3. Flink workers batch events into Parquet files grouped by event time within the hour. These files are great for high-throughput streaming writes, but not for low-latency reads. Enter the Compaction job. Compaction Job to Optimize Reads The compaction job runs daily and merges small Parquet files into a single, optimized daily Parquet file per namespace. title: Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
excerpt: By Prashanth Gedde Narayanaswamy As one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile. A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result. That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way. The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale Bugs Standard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks. While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. A standard 1% sample misses these extreme long-tail sessions entirely. To catch the real bugs, every test run had to execute against a full hour of unsampled production data, along with all the deployment overhead that came with it. The Strategy: Branch-Driven Isolation The biggest win came from a feature in Dataflow , Netflix’s command-line tool for building, testing, and deploying data pipelines. It supports branch-driven development : our workflows run on Maestro ( Netflix’s workflow orchestrator), which schedules and executes the jobs, and they already use a sanitized branch name (the ${dataflow.sanitizedbranch} placeholder). So if I push a branch like pgn/cap-experiment , then the deployed workflow, its tables, and its run namespace all get tagged with that branch name. This eliminates collisions with team members or between my own concurrent runs. With that isolation in place, the model was simple: one branch is one independent experiment . I parameterized the scheduler (cap size, shuffle partitions, heavy-device threshold, feature flags) and gave each variant its own branch and output table. Instead of queuing five sequential tests over 10 hours, I fired off five variants simultaneously against the same time window. Total execution time dropped from the sum of all runs to just the length of the single slowest job. Managing per-branch tables added zero overhead. Dataflow provisions and updates tables automatically from declared schemas without manual DDL. Whenever I modified the event bag structure between experiments, the table schema updated seamlessly, no CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE required. The only real constraint was cluster contention. Because these heavy Spark jobs shared resources with the rest of the company, peak hours sometimes limited me to two concurrent runs instead of five. But even running two or three jobs in parallel was a massive improvement over single-threaded debugging. The key takeaway: don’t focus on making a single multi-hour run faster, build a setup where you can run many experiments simultaneously without them stepping on each other. title: Netflix Conductor: The Next Chapter
excerpt: Netflix Conductor : The Next Chapter by Aravindan Ramkumar on behalf of the Conductor team Conductor is the workflow orchestration engine Netflix uses to stitch micro-services into reliable, observable business processes. If you’ve followed Conductor from the outside, the last thing you heard was probably the note on its GitHub repository : Netflix discontinued maintenance of Conductor OSS to refocus its resources on the internal fork. That announcement marked the end of the open-source chapter, and from the outside it may have looked like the end of the story. It wasn’t. Internally, Conductor never slowed down. If anything, it grew faster, and the demands of that growth pushed us to rebuild it from the ground up. This post is the answer to the natural question that announcement leaves open: what happened to Conductor after that? A lot, it turns out. The clearest way to put it is in terms of growth. Not long ago, Conductor crossing a billion workflow executions in a single year felt like a milestone. Today it clears that bar roughly every quarter , and the monthly volume is still climbing. Sustaining that kind of growth meant rethinking nearly every layer of the system. The data plane it runs on was modernized piece by piece. The evaluation engine was rewritten. The way it allocates work, controls concurrency, and runs compute all changes. The through-line is simple: scale forced a rethink of the evaluation engine and the layers beneath it, and everything else followed. The rest of this post walks through that evolution: how the architecture changed, the performance and scale work at the heart of it, the leap forward in developer experience, and the newer capabilities for controlling how workflows and tasks execute. How Netflix uses Conductor When we last wrote about Conductor, it ran a few hundred workflow definitions for a few dozen teams. That footprint has grown by orders of magnitude. Conductor now backs roughly 200,000 workflow definitions owned by around 150 applications , spanning Content and Studio Engineering, Ads, Games, and more. The runtime side has grown to match. In a typical month it executes on the order of 420 million workflows , and on a given day it runs anywhere from 5 to 20 million , with teams adding hundreds of new workflow types every month. Conductor and the Media Production Suite One of the clearest ways to see what Conductor does is Netflix’s Media Production Suite (MPS) . It’s a set of applications that move production data into the cloud. An average Netflix title generates around 200 terabytes of original camera files, and MPS is what gets that media ingested, validated, transcoded, and delivered to the right people around the world. The multi-step pipelines behind MPS’s workflows (Footage Ingest, Dailies, VFX Pulls, and Conform Pulls) run as Conductor workflows. A dedicated orchestration layer called Studio Orchestrator stitches together the platform services these pipelines depend on, such as asset management, media encoding, and storage, using Conductor under the hood to ensure reliable execution and the durability to recover from the inevitable failures of long-running, distributed work. Beyond the studio: Ads and Games Content engineering is where Conductor started, but it’s no longer the whole story. Two of Netflix’s newer businesses lean on it just as heavily. Netflix Ads has made Conductor a backbone of its programmatic pipelines. Creative ingestion, advertiser-certificate management, and privacy-preserving Data Clean Rooms all run as Conductor workflows. Netflix Games uses Conductor to orchestrate the path a game takes from a partner’s submission to the app stores. When a studio uploads a build, a Conductor pipeline ingests the binary, runs the required validations (for example, iOS privacy-manifest checks), and drives App Store publishing, coordinating steps that span multiple platform services and external stores with the same reliability and visibility the studio pipelines rely on. title: Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations
excerpt: By Kevin Zielnicki, Guy Aridor, Aurélien Bibaut, Allen Tran, Winston Chou, and Nathan Kallus Introduction Personalization is everywhere on the internet. It shapes the products we discover, the stories we read, the music we hear, and the movies and TV shows we watch. At Netflix, personalization has been central to the member experience for decades — from the Netflix Prize to our modern recommender system that helps members navigate a large and constantly changing catalog. But personalization is not only an algorithmic problem, it is also a measurement problem. How do we know how much value personalization creates? More precisely, how do we separate the appeal of a title from the value created by recommending that title to the right member at the right time? In a new article in the International Journal of Industrial Organization — which we are also presenting at this year’s ACM Conference on Economics & Computation (EC ‘26) — we develop a model of member behavior, title choice, and personalized recommendations. The model lets us estimate how recommendations affect both whether members choose to watch and, if so, which titles they choose. In this post, we summarize our approach and main findings. The Measurement Challenge A natural first attempt at valuing recommendations is to ask: what share of viewing comes from titles that were recommended? This is an intuitive metric, but it fails to answer the causal question at hand. The problem is that recommendations are not randomly assigned. A title appears on a member’s homepage precisely because the recommender system predicts that the member might want to watch it. If a member watches that title, was it because the recommendation caused the member to watch it? Or would she have watched it anyway because of her underlying preference for that kind of title? This is the core measurement challenge: recommendations are targeted to demand, so viewing a recommended title combines the effect of personalization with the member’s underlying preferences. One way to solve this would be to run a large experiment that replaces Netflix’s personalized experience with an unpersonalized one. That would create clean variation — but it would also be a poor member experience. Personalization is a central part of how members locate valuable titles in a large catalog, so turning it off broadly is not an acceptable measurement strategy. Instead, we take a hybrid approach. We build a behavioral model that separates members’ underlying preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations. The model uses the natural variation in the recommendation system, for example due to algorithmic exploration, to estimate how recommendations affect choice. Then, to validate the model predictions about title substitutability, we use small-scale A/B tests that “nudge” the salience of a handful of titles exogenously, generating ground-truth substitution patterns for a subset of titles. This lets us combine the scale and richness of modeling with the credibility of experimental evidence. A Model of Member Choice To measure the value of personalization, we need a model of what members would watch under different recommendation systems. Our model treats Netflix viewing as a day-by-day choice process. On each day, a member chooses among the titles available in the catalog, or she chooses not to watch anything. This gives us a concrete target to estimate: the probability that a member watches each title on a given day, as a function of their preferences, their viewing history, and the recommendations they see. A simple version of this model would be too restrictive. It might assume, for example, that removing one title from the catalog shifts viewing toward all other titles in roughly proportional ways. But that isn’t how member choice works. If a member is considering a romantic comedy, the closest substitutes are likely other romantic comedies, not every title on Netflix equally. title: Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications
excerpt: Authors: Divya Gadde , Ko-Jen Hsiao , Dhaval Patel and Moumita Bhattacharya The motivation for building the Netflix Foundation Model for personalization was laid out in this previous blog post. The Netflix homepage is powered by several specialized models and it requires significant time and resources to maintain and continue innovating on these individual models. Therefore, we decided to centralize member preference learning and have one powerful model learned from comprehensive user interaction histories and content data at a large scale and have this model distribute its learnings to other models. The previous two blog posts( 1 , 2 ) focus on the development of the Foundation Model and here we talk about how we integrate the Foundation Model into various applications. We found that there is extensive literature focused on the training and inference of large-scale transformer-based models. However, there remains a significant gap in practical guidance and research on how to effectively and efficiently integrate large models into existing production systems. At Netflix, we experimented with 3 distinct integration approaches — embeddings, subgraph and fine-tuning. The motivation for trying different approaches stems from varying application needs. Specifically, different teams have different latency requirements, tech stack constraints and different appetites for leveraging the full power of a large foundation model. In this blog, we go over the 3 approaches we experimented with and which are now used in production for different use cases. Each integration approach has its own set of motivations, tradeoffs, complexities and learnings. The following sections go into the details of each of these integration approaches. Embeddings from Foundation model Transformer style foundation models naturally lend themselves to generating comprehensive user profile and item representations. Our approach for generating embeddings includes getting the hidden state of the last user event as the profile embedding and weights from the item tower as item embeddings. Netflix has an elaborate set up for refreshing the embeddings every day. First, the Foundation Model is pre-trained from scratch every month. Then, the monthly pre-trained model is fine-tuned everyday based on the latest data. The daily fine-tuning also expands the entity id space to include the newly launching titles. After the daily fine-tuned model is ready, we run batch inference to refresh the profile and item embeddings and publish them to the Embedding Store. An important part of this setup is the embedding stabilization technique ( paper ). When the pretraining job retrains the model from scratch, the embedding spaces between different runs are completely different due to the random initialization in the model. In addition, the embeddings start to drift when the daily job fine-tunes on the latest data, despite the daily fine-tuning job warm-starting from the previous day’s model. Therefore, it is important to map the embeddings generated everyday into the same embedding space, so that downstream models can consume pre-computed embeddings as features. This embedding approach relies heavily on the Embedding Store, which is a feature store specializing in embeddings built by the platform team at Netflix. The embedding store makes producing and consuming embeddings easy by taking care of versioning and timestamping the embeddings. The Embedding Store also provides various interfaces to access the embeddings offline and online. Embedding Store integration This approach is often the initial and most straightforward way for applications to interact with the Foundation Model. Embeddings can serve as powerful features for other models or for candidate generation, helping to retrieve appealing titles for a user or facilitate title-to-title recommendations. title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
excerpt: by Olek Gorajek , Samuel Redai , Yian Shang Intro Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets. Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values. Initial Problem Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required: extensive business knowledge familiarity with experimentation conventions and complex engineering practices This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform. Enter DataJunction To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case. DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers ( Beto Dealmeida ), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet , have been building out the remaining features of the platform. title: Behind the Scenes: Evolving Netflix’s Ads Event Pipeline for Live — Part II
excerpt: By Yogesh Nagarur Introduction In Part 1 of this series , we shared how Netflix built the Ads Event pipeline and approached it as a system design problem: replacing fragmented pipelines with a centralized collection, enrichment, and a standard data contract. The result was Ads Event Publisher, the system that collects ad telemetry from client devices, enriches it with the context of the ad that was actually served, and publishes a single, unified stream of ad events to every downstream consumer: frequency capping, metrics, billing, measurement partners, and reporting. Any member viewing or account details that move through this pipeline end-to-end are encrypted and handled in accordance with Netflix’s strict privacy and security practices to safeguard member PII. If ad serving is the “brain” and ad events are the “heartbeats” that feed it, then enrichment is what gives each heartbeat its meaning, turning a bare “[Somebody] watched an ad to completion” signal into “ this campaign, this creative, at this price, for this break.” Part 1 described that enrichment step as a single box in the architecture. This post is about what was inside that box, and why we rebuilt it. Part 1 ended with a look at what was on the horizon: ads on live streams, de-duplication, and richer data signals. A single project delivered all three by rebuilding the Ads Event Publisher around stateful stream processing. We replaced a database lookup with a real-time streaming join in Apache Flink, which let the system scale for Live, took a dependency off the critical path, and replaced the engine of a high-traffic pipeline without downtime. Let’s dive in. A quick recap: enrichment and the Metadata Registry When an ad is served, the ad server knows everything about it: the campaign, the creative, the price of the impression, the targeting context, and the tracking URLs that measurement partners expect us to fire. The client device, by contrast, knows almost nothing: just an opaque token and when to send each event. Enrichment is the act of reuniting the two. In the architecture from Part 1, that reunion happened through the Ads Metadata Registry , a Key-Value store: When the ad server made a decision, it wrote the metadata for that impression into the registry. It encoded only reference identifiers into the opaque token returned to the device, keeping the token small. Later, when the client fired an event carrying that token, the Ads Event Publisher decoded the token, looked up the metadata in the registry, and stitched the two together into an enriched ad event. This design served us well. The registry was globally replicated, which gave us a useful property almost for free: an event arriving in any region could find its metadata regardless of where the ad was decided. It future-proofed the token against ever-growing metadata, and it carried us through the first phase of Netflix’s advertising growth. The ad server writes per-impression metadata to the globally replicated registry on the serving path, and the Ads Event Publisher reads it back to enrich each client event. But as we looked ahead, especially to ads on live streams, the limits of this design became clear. Why we needed to evolve The forcing function was Live. Netflix’s live slate has grown rapidly, from NFL games to blockbuster fight nights to the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2027 , and viewership keeps growing. That traffic looks nothing like Subscription Video on Demand (SVOD): a single event can surge toward tens of millions of concurrent viewers within minutes, then drain just as fast when it ends. Building the ad pipeline for Live meant building for that trajectory. To see why the old design could not get there, let’s put some numbers on it. When Netflix streamed the Jake Paul vs. Mike Tyson fight to more than 100 million viewers, a single ad break at that scale would generate an enormous volume of ad events.
